newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece gets tough to make grade for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Greece gets tough to make grade for EMU.

text.p: Greece's socialist government vowed on Monday to qualify for European Economic and Monetary Union by 2000 and said it would squeeze more taxes out of the rich in the toughest budget in 15 years.

Goals of the 1997 budget due this week were slashing state spending, ending tax breaks, levying heavier taxes on the rich, limiting state hiring and privatising faster, National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou said.
"The expected slashing of the general government deficit in 1997 constitutes the most ambitious fiscal target of the last 15 years," he told a conference on the economy.
He said the woes of Greece, the European Union's poorest state, were due to a lack of stable and credible policies over the past 20 years. The socialists ruled for much of that time.
A Cambrige-educated economist who has been staunchly pro-EU since assuming his ministry in 1994, Papandoniou said joining EMU was vital to the country's national interests.
"We are not so far behind as to believe we have missed the train. With work, I believe that at the turn of the century we will be in Europe. That is the aim of this government," he said.
His plans sounded ambitious given that Greece is the only EU member that has not fulfilled a single EMU requirement.
Greece has shown little interest in joining other EU states in the Exchange Rate Mechanism, saying it will pursue its "strong drachma" policy to cut inflation.
Prime Minister Costas Simitis vowed last week to impose the necessary measures to put Greece's economic house in order and to have the country in EMU with its EU partners by 2000 or 2001.
Like Papandoniou, he said failure to enter EMU shortly after the official 1999 target date, would condemn Greece to being a second class citizen in the 15-member union.
Simitis took over in January from legendary socialist party founder Andreas Papandreou, whose free-spending policies in the 1980s are often blamed for Greece's present economic weakness.
Sounding more like a neo-conservative than a Papandreou populist, Simitis called early elections and won a four-year mandate in September to impose his economic programme.
In a newspaper interview on Monday, Papandoniou said that EU patience was running out and Athens must do what was necessary to meet the economic criteria agreed in the Maastricht treaty.

"We hope by 1998 to be ready as regards the criteria in the Maastricht treaty - to have achieved inflation close to three percent and brought the debt to three percent of GDP," he said in the interview with 'Ethnos' newspaper.

Failure to get on track by 1998 would risk EU funding and many projects could be delayed, he said. EU funds have poured into Greece to help pay for an array of infrastructure projects such as a new Athens international airport and metro.
Getting such projects finished is vital to Greece's campaign to win the 2004 summer Olympics. Failure to finish the projects would be another blow to the country's already tarnished image.

Reflecting Simitis's efforts to lead Greece out of its past isolation, Papandoniou said cutting inflation and interest rates would "strengthen our participation in a large group of industrialised nations, which have credibility and power".
Papandoniou said the rich and powerful must help pay for EU convergence and Greece's notorious tax evasion, especially among the wealthy, would be curtailed.

"The affluent and high income earners manage to evade taxes in various ways," he said. "There are significant margins to cut the debt and provide basic social justice. The affluent and high income earners will pay."
But he also said lower wage earners must shoulder their share, rejecting calls to readjust income brackets and to raise the threshold for tax-free income.
